reading.title: Reading a vineyard planting record
reading.text: An agricultural student compares the vineyard's written planting records. The list names Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir as grape varieties, not guaranteed flavors. A second block contains Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Syrah and Malbec. Another block contains Tempranillo and Zinfandel. The vine is the grape plant; a trellis supports it, and a row is a line of plantings. Terroir concerns the growing place's combined environmental and human context. A slope is inclined ground, not necessarily a mountain. The student asks which record supports a variety's identity. Similar grape clusters can be difficult to distinguish in a photograph, and location alone does not establish the variety. The lesson practices interpreting agricultural descriptions without prescribing cultivation or consumption.

reading.title: Discussing the vine's annual cycle
reading.text: The student follows a narrated annual-cycle display. Irrigation supplies water, while the canopy is the vine's leaves and shoots. Root stock forms the rooted base used in grafting, the joining of compatible plant parts. Pruning removes selected growth. Bud break starts new growth from dormant buds; flowering produces flowers, and veraison marks the onset of grape ripening. Harvest gathers the crop. Crush refers here to the stage of breaking grape berries for processing. The growing season is the active growth period, whereas dormancy involves greatly reduced activity. Frost protection names measures intended to reduce freezing damage. Netting can help protect the crop, and hand picking means collecting it manually. The student discusses the terms without treating the display as advice for a particular site or a universal schedule.

reading.title: Identifying assigned industry roles
reading.text: A fictional business chart distinguishes several wine-industry roles. Vintner can mean a producer or seller of wine. The viticulturist specializes in grape growing, while the cellar master supervises cellar operations. A sommelier specializes in wine service and selection. The vineyard manager coordinates cultivation and maintenance; the winemaker produces wine. The harvest crew gathers grapes. An enologist studies wine and its production, and a cooper makes or repairs wooden barrels. A négociant buys grapes, juice or wine from others and markets wine under the business's name. Responsibilities can overlap, so the student checks the chart's actual assignments. Neither clothing nor a barrel in the background establishes a person's occupation. The vocabulary supports professional reading without requiring a learner to drink or work in the industry.
